newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia share bulls awaiting real economic change.
newsitem.headline: Russia share bulls awaiting real economic change.

text.p: The Russian market is showing sparks of life after a two-month lull, but fund managers invested in Russia on Wednesday saw major new allocations being held back for another month at least.

Cautious major institutional investors with the funds to move the market, as in January and February when leading shares rose about 75 percent, were seen waiting for the results of economic reforms and improving external factors.
"I see no major (market) changes in the next month," said Paul Leander-Engstrom, a partner at Westman Leander-Engstrom which manages the $110 million Russian Prosperity Fund.
Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, the two first deputy prime ministers leading Russian economic reforms, need time to prove they can produce change rather than announce it, he said.
"People will probably say it is time to increase exposure when Chubais and Nemtsov can point to some results," he said.
Market bellwether Unified Energy System (UES) EESR.RTS, the national electric company which is a top target for reforms, hit a record $0.2679 on Wednesday after Tuesday's $0.2380 close.
Shares have been drifting for about two months.
The Russian Trading System 22-share index jumped to 316.58 at midday on Wednesday from 305.53. It was under 200 at the end of last year and hit a high of 349.29 on February 20.
But total market turnover, which usually rises in a bull market, remained light and traders said buyers were stocking up before May holidays when shares would be even harder to find.

The Russian market is often driven upward by liquidity crises, as during the new year when major new allocations chased limited shares for sale. Leander-Engstrom said even leading shares had been hard to find in the down market, indicating investor support not evident in prices.

Clariden Bank Executive Vice President Beat Wittmann, chief investment officer of the bank's $15-$20 million Russia Fund, said many investors were looking for a decisive move such as the breakup of UES or telecoms holding Svyazinvest.
"The trigger point is the breakup of such a thing," he said.
"There would be a total re-evaluation. I would have no problem seeing the market between 30 and 60 percent higher -- because you will not be able to find a seller."
But Russian government leaders have said they will not break up its leading companies and are looking at changing regulations and personnel. "Changing people is not enough," Wittman said.

He said funds were also watching for Russia's listing on investable indexes by the International Finance Corporation and Morgan Stanley, expected in May, though managers said listing effects would be felt over a number of months.
Russia has begun to correlate with global markets as major Western investors have increased stakes and traders say calm on Wall Street is necessary for a Russian rally.

Pioneer First Investment Group reseach director Christopher Smart said major funds would move slowly in any case, not reacting to single events or announcements, though he expected an upturn in the market over the next couple of months.
"(A breakup) might be a trigger for the hot money -- the hedge funds -- but the more mainstream money that has begun to come in really wants to know more what it is buying," he said.

"A government announcement -- 'here is what we are going to do with natural monopolies today' -- is not going to lead to a new wave of investment tomorrow. Governments in general and Russia in particular have a habit of changing their plans."
But he said he expected an upturn in the market over the next two months. "The nervousness at the beginning of the year is fading, and the sky's the limit."
